frames.narration: User 42 buys something for 30. The event reaches the stream. The feature 'spend so far' is defined once, and the same pipeline will compute it for both stores.
The pipeline appends the new value to the offline history, with the time it became true. The old row (120, valid from 09:40) is not changed.
The same pipeline writes the newest value to the online store. A write older than the stored one would be ignored, so out-of-order delivery cannot move a value back.
At 10:05 a payment by user 42 needs a fraud score. The model service reads the features with one batched lookup and gets 150 within a couple of milliseconds, without touching any source database.

Weeks later, the payment turns out to be fraud. That label has time 10:05. The training job asks for the feature as it was at 10:05, and a plain 'latest' join would instead give today's spend, which the model could not have known.
The as-of join finds the last row of user 42 at or before 10:05 in the offline history: 150, valid since 10:00. Later rows (for example 310 at 16:20) are ignored.

The model learned from 150, exactly the number it saw when it scored that payment. If a bug in the definition is found later, a backfill replays the raw events through the same pipeline and writes a new version of the history, which gives the same result every time it runs.
